item.title: Do Psychedelics Need the Trip to Treat Depression?
item.description:
Psychedelics

Do Psychedelics Need the Trip to Treat Depression?

Scientists are testing whether they can keep the medicine and lose the trip.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • We don’t know if the psychedelic trip is necessary for psychiatric benefit from hallucinogens.
  • A trip may loosen rigid brain networks, but plasticity alone isn’t automatically therapeutic.
  • Animal studies suggest that antidepressant effects with hallucinogens can occur without the trip.
  • Only human trials can tell us what’s lost—or gained—when the psychedelic trip is removed.

One question may determine whether psychedelics ever move from specialized research centers into psychiatric offices. Does the patient need to trip for the treatment to work?

This is not a minor issue. Hallucinations are unpredictable. Increasing brain plasticity is not automatically therapeutic. Psychedelics may open a therapeutic window, but they cannot control what comes through. Selecting the right patient, preparation, setting, safety and monitoring, therapy, and follow-up may determine how much the experience helps. All of that is much more involved and costly than prescribing a pill.

Psychedelics are moving toward mainstream psychiatry, led by psilocybin for depression. Clinical trials use synthetic psilocybin with a known dose and purity—not an unpredictable mushroom. But standardized psilocybin is still a hallucinogen.

Scientists may have managed to strip the hallucinations away from therapeutic compounds in animal studies, but it is not looking that simple for humans. In clinical trials, patients who have the strongest, most meaningful trips usually see the best results. That doesn’t automatically mean the trip is causing the cure, but it makes it pretty hard to argue that the experience doesn’t matter.

In a 2026 Nature Medicine article, NYU’s Josh Siegel and his colleagues proposed a two-stage model. First, the psychedelic disturbs the brain’s usual organization. Then it opens a temporary period of increased plasticity, when learning and change may become easier.

Psilocybin is rapidly converted to psilocin, which activates serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, particularly on cortical pyramidal neurons. An international analysis of 11 imaging datasets involving five psychedelics found increased communication between higher-order networks and systems controlling sensation and movement. The brain’s usual boundaries became less rigid.

For a depressed patient, that disruption may make the depressed brain less certain that its glass-empty view of the world is the only possible one. Not being depressed becomes imaginable. But what produced the improvement: the neurobiology, the trip, or both?

Clinical Evidence and the Blinding Problem

In a 2026 Maudsley NHS trial, 60 patients with treatment-resistant depression received either 25 mg of COMP360 psilocybin or placebo, along with preparation, dosing support, and integration. After three weeks, the psilocybin group improved by 10.41 points more on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale. Benefits persisted at six weeks. Impressive. But every patient who received psilocybin correctly guessed that they had received the drug—so much for blinding.

Stacey Armstrong’s 2026 open-label pilot study treated 12 veterans with severe, treatment-resistant PTSD. They received two psilocybin sessions surrounded by approximately 16 hours of preparation and integration therapy. Nine were in remission one month later. Again, impressive. But symptoms had already started improving during preparation. Patients who improved more before receiving psilocybin also did better afterward. The open study supports psilocybin treatment but can’t tell us which part worked—or whether the trip was essential.

We Have Tried This Before

Psychiatry has pursued a similar goal with electroconvulsive therapy (ECT): keep its remarkable antidepressant effect while reducing memory loss, cognitive burden, anesthesia requirements, and fear. Modern anesthesia, unilateral electrode placement, and ultrabrief-pulse stimulation have made ECT safer and easier to tolerate. But its extraordinary efficacy has not been reproduced without inducing a therapeutic seizure.

ECT taught us an important lesson: Keeping the cure while removing the cost is harder than it sounds.

Can Chemistry Keep the Medicine and Lose the Trip?

A 2025 meta-analysis found that the intensity of the psychedelic experience was associated with greater clinical improvement, especially in mood disorders. But association is not causation.

A 2026 study from David Olson’s group at UC Davis makes the question easier to test. The investigators deconstructed LSD’s four-ring structure and synthesized nine simpler analogs. Removing different structural elements changed activity at receptors associated with psychedelic effects. Two compounds showed less hallucinogenic potential in preclinical tests.

This is very clever medicinal chemistry. It is not clinical proof.

None of these compounds has been shown to treat depression, anxiety, addiction, or any other disorder in humans. Their immediate value is in future experiments, as deconstructed LSD may allow scientists to compare plasticity with and without the trip.

Could We Produce the Experience Without the Psychedelic?

Stanford researchers approached the problem from the opposite direction. Instead of removing the experience from the drug, they asked whether they could produce a meaningful altered experience without a psychedelic.

They tested whether a brief, controlled dream during emergence from propofol anesthesia could reproduce part of the experience associated with psychedelics. Their five-step protocol produced dream recall in 69 percent of 452 surgical patients. Of the dreams recalled, 86 percent were rated positive or somewhat positive.

This was a feasibility study. It did not show that dreaming treats PTSD. That study is underway. But if a structured altered experience improves PTSD without a psychedelic, the experience may be more than pharmacologic noise.

Nitrous oxide (NO) offers another clue. Washington University investigators have taken nitrous oxide research from a small proof-of-concept trial to dose-ranging and repeated-treatment studies examining suicidality and brain connectivity.

Nitrous oxide briefly alters consciousness and changes medial limbic, default-mode, salience, reward, and cognitive-control networks. NO leaves the lungs within minutes, while its antidepressant effects may last for days or weeks.

The experience ends. The brain effect does not.

This does not prove that the nitrous oxide experience is irrelevant. It does warn us not to mistake the trip for the mechanism. The trip may be the driver, an amplifier, or simply a passenger. We just do not know.

This argument predates today’s psychedelic renaissance. In 1956, Alcoholics Anonymous cofounder Bill Wilson took LSD under medical supervision. Wilson believed the experience might help some alcoholics reach the spiritual awakening central to his own recovery. Many AA members strongly objected. LSD never became part of AA. Fellowship, sponsorship, repeated practice, and service did.

Perhaps that was Bill W.’s unintended lesson: A drug may produce a powerful experience, but an experience is not recovery. What follows the trip may matter more than the trip.

Biology and Experience May Work Together

A psychedelic trip is not necessarily pleasant. It may include fear, grief, loss of control, hallucinations, and painful memories. But a difficult psychedelic experience is not necessarily experienced as harmful or ultimately judged negatively.

In a survey of 1,993 adults describing their worst psilocybin experience, 39 percent ranked it among the five most challenging experiences of their lives. Nevertheless, 84 percent reported benefiting from it, and 46 percent said they would repeat the same session—including the difficult parts.

Would patients want or accept psychedelic-inspired treatment without the trip? We do not know. Some might prefer it. Others may believe the experience is the treatment.

If scientists can preserve therapeutic plasticity while eliminating hallucinations, psychedelic-inspired medicines could become safer, cheaper, and easier to deliver. But removing the trip may also remove part of the benefit.

Depression is not simply abnormal circuitry, rigidity, or receptor signaling. It includes hopelessness, anhedonia, rigid expectations, painful memories, self-absorption, and loss of meaning. Psychedelic treatment may loosen the connections, but experience may determine what replaces it.

Until human trials provide a clear answer, we should resist two temptations: romanticizing the trip and declaring it unnecessary too soon.

item.title: Yes, You Should Be Afraid of Death
item.description:
Fear

Yes, You Should Be Afraid of Death

But you mustn’t let death spoil your life.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Death may harm us by depriving us of the life we might otherwise have lived.
  • Fear of death can consume the very life it seeks to protect.
  • We must accept mortality to prevent death from defeating us twice.
Orpheus and Eurydice seeking to flee the Underworld.
Source: Wikimedia commons/W Poynter/public domain.

Most attempts to console us about death begin by denying that it is an evil. But what if it is an evil—and our task is not to deny this, but to prevent the fear of death from spoiling the life that remains to us?

Is Death an Evil?

In 1970, the philosopher Thomas Nagel published a short paper entitled "Death," in which he asked: If death is the permanent end of our existence, is it an evil?

There are, at least for the non-believer, only two possible answers. Either death is an evil because it deprives us of life, or it is a mere blank because there is no one left to suffer this deprivation.

If death is an evil, it is not because of any unpleasant attribute that it has, such as eternal torment, but because of what it takes away: life itself. For Nagel, the bare experience of life is intrinsically valuable, regardless of the balance of its good and bad elements.

The longer we live, the more life we accumulate. Death, in contrast, cannot be accumulated. It is not, as Nagel puts it, "an evil of which Shakespeare has so far received a larger portion than Proust." If death is an evil, this is not because it condemns us to a longer or shorter period of non-existence, but because it deprives us of the life that we might otherwise have lived.

The Epicurean Case Against Fearing Death

More than two thousand years before Nagel, Epicurus offered two famous reasons for not fearing death.

First, there is no subject left to suffer it. So long as we are alive, death has not arrived; as soon as death arrives, we are no longer alive. There seems, therefore, to be no time at which the evil of death can befall us.

Second, we do not regard the infinitely long period before our birth as an evil. Why, then, should we regard the period after our death any differently?

These arguments are known respectively as the "no subject of harm" argument and the "symmetry" argument.

Nagel answers that the good or evil that befalls us depends not only on our momentary experience, but also on our history and possibilities. Something can harm us even if we never become aware of it. If people betray or ridicule us behind our backs, their actions may constitute a misfortune for us even if we never discover what happened.

Similarly, death can harm us without leaving anyone behind to experience the harm. Its evil consists in the cancellation of our possibilities: the relationships, projects, pleasures, and discoveries that might otherwise have formed part of our life.

The period before our birth did not deprive us of anything because our life had not yet begun. But death interrupts a life already in progress. The symmetry between prenatal and posthumous non-existence is therefore less perfect than it first appears.

Death Kills Us Twice

If Nagel is right, death is an evil insofar as it deprives us of life. But it gets worse.

Death not only deprives us of life; it also compels us to spend that very life in the mostly unconscious fear of being deprived of it. Much of our anxiety, and much of the frantic activity with which we seek to escape it, may stem from our fear of death.

We pursue wealth, status, achievement, or youth as though they might protect us from mortality. We keep ourselves busy so that we need not think about where all our busyness is leading. Yet the more life we sacrifice to the fear of losing life, the more completely death has already defeated us.

Death, therefore, kills us twice: once when it ends our life, and again, by anticipation, when it prevents us from making the most of the life that we have.

A Necessary but Dangerous Fear

The fear of death is not irrational. If life is valuable, then it is reasonable to fear being deprived of it. The problem is not that we fear death, but that the fear becomes so great, so diffuse, or so deeply buried that it diminishes the very thing it seeks to preserve.

We may be able to postpone death by a few years, but there is nothing we can do to avoid it. In the words of Epicurus, "It is possible to provide security against other ills, but as far as death is concerned, we men live in a city without walls."

All that we can do is come to terms with death in the hope of preventing it from preventing us from living.

item.title: 25 Years Later, Do You Remember 9/11?
item.description:
Memory

25 Years Later, Do You Remember 9/11?

Most people have memories of 9/11, but are those memories accurate?

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Most people can still remember hearing the news about 9-11.
  • The surprisingly detailed and long-lasting memories reflect normal processes rather than a special mechanism.
  • Flashbulb memories often include errors although people remain confident in the accuracy of their memories.
  • Politicians also have errors in their memories, possibly reflecting political goals guiding reconstuction.

After 25 years, do you remember where you were when you learned about September 11th, 2001? As we encounter another anniversary of 9-11, you probably find those memories coming to mind. Most people recall hearing the news. Your memory may feel particularly clear and accurate. My memory of hearing the news feels real and complete. But why do we remember these events and are our memories actually accurate?

Old Enough to Remember

If you were older than 4 or 5, you probably remember hearing the news, based on Winograd and Killinger's (1983) research on the memories of hearing about John F. Kennedy’s assassination. People who were in the first few years of life, they didn’t recall much – evidence of childhood amnesia, perhaps. But most people over the age of 4 had some memories. For 9-11, if you’re older than 30, you probably have a memory. Why do these memories stand out?

Why Do We Recall Hearing about 9-11?

At one time, the argument was that these memories were unique. Brown and Kulik (1977) proposed that a special memory mechanism was involved in creating such "flashbulb" memories. They likened it to taking a picture, the flashbulb as a metaphor. They made the argument that these memories were long-lasting and detailed—seemingly more than other memories. Psychologists have noted that hearing the news of shocking and important events results in these types of memories, at least since the assassination of Abraham Lincoln (Colgrove, 1899).

But it is unlikely that we need a special mechanism to explain these long-lasting memories. Instead, these flashbulb memories probably reflect normal memory processes (Neisser, 1982/2000). The events are important. Importance means that we think and talk about these events more than other sorts of events. Rehearsal improves memory. We also track the news about the events as they develop over hours and days. Certainly, we learned more about 9-11 in the hours, days, and weeks after the event occurred. It led to dramatic changes in US and world politics. We are also encouraged to rehearse our memories every year at this time, whether through memorials, more news reporting, or posts such as this one.

These flashbulb memories also have simple and clear retrieval cues. You only need to ask someone where they were on 9-11. It is a reminder that only leads to one event, making it easy to bring your story to mind. Asking you to recall other memories from 2001 may bring little information to mind, reflecting a lack of clear retrieval cues.

Are These Flashbulb Memories Accurate?

Although these memories often feel clear, complete, and accurate, they are no more accurate than any other memory. To investigate accuracy, researchers first collect people’s recollections of how they learned surprising news the day after the event. Months or years later, they again ask people to recall the event. The researchers then compare the memories to see if people provide a consistent narrative.

Simply put, people make errors in remembering (Hirst et al., 2009; Hirst et al., 2015; Neisser & Harsh, 1992; Talarico & Rubin, 2003; Winningham et al., 2000). These flashbulb memories are no more accurate than memories of personal events, although people are more confident in their flashbulb memories (Talarico & Rubin, 2003).

Flashbulb memories also seem to settle into a narrative that people may stick with over long periods of time (Winningham et al, 2000). Neisser and Harsh (1992) found that memories changed from the original to a later recollection, but that the memories stabilized over time (see also Hirst et al., 2015). In some ways, people talk and develop their stories. They may then settle into the version of their memory that sticks afterwards (Drivdahl & Hyman, 2014).

All memories are constructed. We encode limited aspects of any event. As we later recall, we fill in the missing pieces. We may also develop a narrative based on our audience. With each retelling, we may hear other information from other sources. With flashbulb memories, we often reconstruct our memories to match our normal way of receiving news. Our memories are fluid, changing as we retell them in different contexts.

Politicians and False Flashbulb Memories

In many ways, politicians are just like the rest of us. We shouldn’t expect a politician’s memories to be completely accurate. They also reconstruct their memories. With flashbulb memories for 9-11, however, we may need to be particularly careful. Memories are reconstructed based on the goals of the person remembering. Political figures have a variety of goals in telling a story and they may tell a version of their 9-11 memories that fit with broader narratives. They probably aren’t intentionally lying. More likely, they are reconstructing a version of the past that fits with their political goals.

George W. Bush, for example, has often provided a memory that can’t be true. He has claimed that he saw a video of the first plane crashing into a tower before later being told about the second plane. No such videos were available during that time, so he could not have learned that way (Greenberg, 2004).

A current politician has made claims about seeing huge crowds of people in New Jersey celebrating the 9-11 terrorist attacks (something that didn’t happen) and stated that he was helping clean up shortly after the attacks and being carried to safety by firefighters (something that has never been documented; Stein, 2026).

The errors in our memories of hearing about the 9-11 attacks are not particularly important. Most of our memory errors are mistakes that don’t change the basic story. But for politicians, take their memories of hearing the news with a grain of salt. They are telling stories that fit political goals.

item.title: How to Handle Criticism Without Becoming Defensive
item.description:
Relationships

How to Handle Criticism Without Becoming Defensive

6 ways to make partners feel safe

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Defensiveness is an evolutionary holdover, not a character flaw.
  • Couples who want lasting intimacy must consciously override biological defensiveness.
  • We need tools in order to receive information without an emotional charge.
  • Properly framed, the intent of criticism is often to help improve a relationship.

Many people come into my office believing that defensiveness (one of the Gottmans’ dreaded four horsemen) is a personal failing; however, you may be relieved to learn that defensiveness is actually an evolutionary holdover rather than a character flaw. Historically, criticism signaled an enemy, so building defenses—sometimes even attacking them before they attacked you—was functional for survival. Unfortunately, that defensiveness is dysfunctional for love.

Whereas the Gottmans believe that contempt is the most lethal of the four horsemen, relationship expert Dr. Warren Farrell believes that defensiveness is the single biggest barrier to a happy relationship. In his book Role Mate to Soul Mate, Dr. Farrell posits that couples who want lasting intimacy must consciously override this biological defensiveness since willpower alone rarely calms a nervous system that has already been piqued. What Farrell offers to make partners feel safe is six mindsets designed to interrupt the defensive reflex before it hijacks a conversation.

Here are Farrell’s six mindsets of receptivity

  • Die for Partner: before listening, ask yourself whether you would risk your life for this person; if the answer is yes, hearing their complaint costs you comparatively little.
  • The Love Guarantee: treat listening as an investment rather than a sacrifice and know that the safety you offer your partner’s feelings tends to come back to you as love.
  • Cinematic Immersion: stay immersed in your partner’s story the way you would stay immersed in a film, without arguing with the plot or defending yourself against it.
  • Attach or Detach: notice the instant a rebuttal starts forming, detach from it, and reattach to what your partner is actually saying, using a pause word like “Hold” if needed.
  • Stream: imagine any anger or distortion in your partner’s words as “pollution” passing through a stream and use your own calm attention to filter out the pollution.
  • Eye Contact: offer supportive eye contact only once you can genuinely receive what’s coming, since eye contact offered too early can invite vulnerability before you’re ready to meet it without defensiveness.

What I like about the six mindsets is that they don’t ask anyone to pointlessly try harder to stay calm. Instead, the mindsets target specific points in the defensive sequence: Die for Partner and the Love Guarantee lower the stakes before the conversation starts, Attach or Detach and Stream give a listener something concrete to do the moment they feel themselves shift from receiving to defending, Cinematic Immersion focuses on distilling the raw plot or information, and Eye Contact comes last since, if offered too early, it can be unsettling.

I worked with a husband who didn’t understand why every attempt by his wife to raise a concern resulted in a shouting match. Like most of us, he genuinely believed he was a good listener, right up until the point that a criticism registered in his subconscious as a verbal dagger, at which point something more primordial than his good intentions took over. I introduced Farrell’s “Cinematic Immersion” technique and asked the husband to picture his wife’s “observation” (complaint) the way he would watch a film in a movie theater—staying immersed in the plot rather than treating every line like Freddy Krueger is hiding in a closet behind him.

What he had been reacting to was not the plot; it was his own emotional charge from some subconscious triggering that something his wife said or did—her tone, her sigh, her furrowed brow, the exasperated pause before she spoke, her folded arms, an eye roll.... Once he learned to separate the charge from the plot, he found he could watch the story unfold without needing to defend himself against it in real time.

In session, I now walk nearly every couple through Farrell’s six mindsets, which gives their nervous systems somewhere to put their outdated alarms so that the information underneath has a chance to land. If it’s left unaddressed and festers into a pattern, defensiveness doesn’t just derail one conversation; it teaches both partners that it’s not safe to be honest.

Couples should rehearse these mindsets to remember something they may forget: their partner is a member of their tribe, and they are safe with them. And it’s in everyone’s best interest within the tribe to be vulnerable with each other, because it builds trust and reinforces secure attachment. The less defensive they are, the more capable they are of receiving information. Suggestions stop sounding like accusations, feedback stops sounding like failure, and criticism becomes what it was always meant to be: one person trying to help improve the relationship.

item.title: The Psychology of Asking Your Partner for Help
item.description:
Relationships

The Psychology of Asking Your Partner for Help

Why does care feel like a threat to some?

Posted September 11, 2026

One of the recurring types of clients I see is hyper-independent people who can do and manage absolutely everything on their own. Yet, the very thing that could be the pinnacle of freedom in their life is the source of fatigue and the feeling of loneliness.

They consistently struggle to ask their partner for help or let them in their world, which causes distance and alienation within the relationship. This hyper-independence is often a sign of being exposed to smothering care early in life.

In 1966, psychologist Jack Brehm described a curious paradox: when a person's freedom is restricted in childhood, even with the best intentions in the caregiver’s mind, the child tends to grow into an adult who actively pushes help away and does things on their own(1). Even at the cost of inconvenience.

Some parents offer help by correcting their children a lot. For instance, taking over a task the child was already attempting: putting on socks, tying their shoelaces, remaking the bed after the child in a "better" way. It sends the message "you don't do things as well as I do." And this kind of care brings a competition of comparisons in which the child always loses to an adult.

Another example is deciding what’s best for their child on behalf of their child, while dismissing the child’s wishes. A teenager wants to take an art elective, but the parent enrolls them in an extra math class instead and tells them afterward: "It would be better for you."

Or a pretty common one, nagging the child about organizing his or her room and keeping it neat at all times, as if the child cannot have any autonomy of creative chaos on their own, including in their own space.

While parents carry a responsibility and teach their children how to adapt to the adult world (hopefully, and provided that they are well-adapted themselves), the incessant acts of behavioral control, guilt-induction, shaming or love-withdrawal if the child doesn't do things to a parent's liking can be masked as care.

Leonard Berkowitz's research found that increased pressure to receive aid reduces a person's willingness to accept help from the person pressuring them. (4) So, if the parent pressures the child into receiving care or help, as the parent sees fit, the child can become averse to any form of help, care, or support over time. And develop hyper-autonomy.

Moreover, research shows that children who have experienced conditional help grow into adults who suffer from physiological stress when they receive help or caring support. Their heart rate spikes, their muscles tense, and they feel a sudden physical urge to escape. (1, 5)

In order for help or care to be accepted well — or for someone to ask for it proactively — several conditions need to be in place:

1. Help needs to be offered from a position of equality

People are more likely to accept help if it is offered by equals. (2) In the case of children, even though parents are not on equal footing with their children, when a child feels respected by their parent and treated as a person in their own right, they are far more likely to accept the parent's help and be grateful for it in the long run.

The same dynamic runs in a relationship between partners.

Jack's job is the one the family moves for, so Lucie gives up hers to follow. Now she's underemployed, and he covers most of the bills. He's sending the message: "Don't worry, I've got us." However, when she talks about missing her job and wants to resume working in new circumstances, Jack is dismissive about it. "I earn more, you earn less in any case."

Her needs are unacknowledged and his help comes from above. It's unequal and it breeds resentment in Lucie. Jack is convinced that she has to be grateful for his contribution, refusing to admit that his help is offered in an atmosphere of superiority that fuels dissatisfaction in the relationship.

2. Help needs to support self-competence

Fisher et al. noted that people refuse help when it evokes in them the "feelings of failure, inferiority, and dependency." (2) Kelley also found that when the help recipient concludes that his or her need was caused by external factors — the task is difficult and many people struggle to do it — they are far more likely to accept (and ask for) help. (6) And vice versa: when the need for help feels like the manifestation of one's own incompetence or inadequacy (as with the example above of tying shoelaces), the recipient abstains from getting help.

In couple dynamics, it might show up in something as ordinary as planning a trip. A spouse books the flights: business class, paid for, done! And says: "It's faster if I just do it alone." What could have been a nice surprise:

a) took away the couple's enjoyment and the bonding activity of ordering the tickets together,
b) raised an implicit question: whose judgment gets to stand?

The booking isn't the problem here. The problem is that the decision was made alone, and the other partner is handed a finished fact, as if they are inadequate to be involved, and should only be grateful for the outcome.

3. Balance of power between the giver and receiver

In some families, children are subjected to "parentification:" the child is expected to comfort their parent, to guess their thoughts, to not be too much of a burden, to emotionally care for the parent. In other words, to do what the parent is supposed to do for the child.

In such cases, the child might develop mistrust toward those offering help, because the child imbibed that help and care, when it comes, always comes with strings attached and an induction of guilt.

As I write in my article "Understanding Our Inner Child in the Struggle for Real Love", the roles often flip within couple relationships as well. We want our partners to love and care for us like children, but to treat us like adults. We regress and project parental roles onto them.

This creates a lot of confusion around asking for help. Druian et al. (3) showed in their experiments that adults are very reluctant to ask for help from children, even when children are presented as of equal ability (e.g., in spelling), as it impinges upon their power status.

Therefore, if one partner is unconsciously taking on the psychological role of a child (they want to be the center of attention, pampered and coddled, have the right to play the helplessness card at any time, to be naive, shed responsibility, etc.), the balance of asking for and giving help goes awry.

In conclusion, independence and autonomy are wonderful for an adult. However, when they become "hyper," when they serve as a defense against losing oneself they prevent you from asking and accepting help from your partner, from relaxing, resting and bonding within a relationship.

What's important to understand here is that even fiercely independent persons still long for care, help and support. They just don't know how to receive it, and are afraid to ask for it from their partner.

They don't really know what care or help looks like without suffocation. And this is one of the things that therapy helps uncover and rebuild: the kind of care that is emotionally safe for you, rather than depleting.

item.title: Are We All a Little Bit Narcissistic?
item.description:
Narcissism

Are We All a Little Bit Narcissistic?

Harmful behavior is common, but it doesn’t always signal a diagnosis.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Most people can display selfish, defensive, or narcissistic traits at times without meeting criteria for NPD.
  • Accountability, self-reflection, and willingness to change are important when evaluating harmful behavior.
  • We don’t need to diagnose someone to recognize that their behavior is harmful or abusive.

Most of us have probably behaved selfishly at some point in our lives. We have made a conversation about ourselves when someone else needed support. We have struggled to empathize with someone because we were too caught up in our own hurt. We have become defensive when confronted with something we did wrong. Maybe we have even tried a little too hard to explain why something wasn’t really our fault.

Source: AI-Generated / Image created by ChatGPT

Does that make us narcissists? Probably not.

One of the problems with the way we talk about narcissism today is that the term has become shorthand for almost any behavior we don’t like. An ex who cheated is a narcissist. Someone who talks about themselves too much is a narcissist. A difficult parent is a narcissist. Someone who refuses to apologize? Definitely a narcissist.

Spend enough time on social media, and it can start to seem as though everyone has narcissistic personality disorder. But narcissistic traits and narcissistic personality disorder are not the same thing.

Narcissistic Traits Exist on a Spectrum

Most of us can and probably will exhibit a lack of empathy or even some narcissistic traits at one or more points in our lives. Human beings are imperfect. We can be selfish, defensive, insensitive, jealous, attention-seeking, or lacking in empathy at times without meeting the criteria for a personality disorder. The difference between a rare trait and actual narcissism is a consistent lack of empathy or understanding of how one’s actions affect others. Most people can look back after the heat of an argument has subsided and see how they might have been hurtful, but people without empathy are incapable of considering remorse.

“Am I narcissistic?” you might ask yourself. If you find yourself asking this question about your relationship, you are likely exhibiting normal self-reflection. This is not to say that you are immune to occasionally narcissistic actions. We are all capable of such actions at some point in our life. The difference is that if we can recognize it, take ownership, and consciously do better, we have less risk of doing further harm.

As a psychotherapist, I try to find the “why” of certain behaviors and their intentions for the relationship. I encourage people to look at patterns. When you recognize that you have hurt someone, what happens next? Are you able to acknowledge it without immediately explaining why it was really their fault? Can you tolerate hearing how your behavior affected another person? Can you apologize? And, perhaps most importantly, can you change your behavior?

Using Labels Loosely Can Cause Harm

Using medical terminology, no matter how colloquialized, has the impact of pathologizing. Just as all differing opinions are not gaslighting, not all people with a lack of empathy can be classified as having a full personality disorder. Even still, not all people with narcissistic personality disorder are cruel or malicious.

These days, it seems that everyone with an honorary degree in armchair psychology from the University of Google feels qualified to diagnose others as narcissists. Still, in reality, few of these casual claims of NPD are legitimate. Being a narcissist is more than just being self-centered.

As with all mental health diagnoses, ambiguity about the term has allowed social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok to become opportunities to go viral with unqualified diagnoses. As a therapist, I am happy that society is having conversations about mental health and that many of my patients have found terms and explanations for their experiences. At the same time, their frequent overuse and watering down can make them feel less powerful.

So, Are We All a Little Bit Narcissistic?

Most of us will behave selfishly sometimes. Most of us will become defensive. We will have moments when empathy is difficult because we are overwhelmed by our own emotions. And most of us will eventually hurt someone we care about, even when we never intended to.

The important distinction is what happens when we’re confronted with the impact of our behavior. Can we listen? Can we reflect? Can we take responsibility? And can we actually change what we do next time? If so, this is likely part of being human. If not, then maybe it is a sign of something deeper.

Excerpted, in part, from my book Invisible Bruises: How a Better Understanding of the Patterns of Domestic Violence Can Help Survivors Navigate the Legal System.

item.title: How Our Senses Soak Up the Wonder and Vitality of Nature
item.description:
Environment

How Our Senses Soak Up the Wonder and Vitality of Nature

"Sensoria" helps us deepen our sensual engagements with the world.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • This collection of beautifully written essays can help readers appreciate the wonder and vitality of nature.
  • What would it be like to see polarized light like a shrimp or taste the world with your arms as an octopus?
  • We need to learn humility and respect for all that developed before us, the beings who can be our teachers.
Source: Willemijn Doelman/Pexels

Every now and again a book comes along that can truly transform how we interact with other animals and nature—how we absorb the world into our senses, bodies, hearts, and minds and deeply rewild ourselves. One such volume is a highly acclaimed collection of interdisciplinary essays and poetry by leading scholars, co-edited by Gavin Van Horn (book co-editor), Bruce Jennings, and Heather Swan (poetry editor), titled Sensoria: Attending to the Wonder and Vitality of Nature.1

In this remarkable collection of writings, you will read about a wide array of topics ranging “from the mating calls of chorus frogs to insect olfaction to elephant funerary rites to the memory-rich tastes of place, Sensoria offers an immersion in the sensual experiences of seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling—and their interactions, combinations, and more-than-human manifestations.” Here’s what Gavin Van Horn and Heather Swan had to say about their work of stretching the moral imagination about human relationships with the nonhuman world.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you and your co-editors compile the essays for Sensoria?

Gavin Van Horn: When we engage the natural world, we might do so at arm’s length, considering this animate planet intellectually, philosophically, or as an object. This book aims to turn attention back to the body—all our senses—and our capacities to be in communication with the natural world. The more-than-human world is wildly diverse in terms of other creatures’ ways of perceiving, and their capacities often exceed our own or are totally different in quality. What would it be like to see polarized light like a mantis shrimp? Taste the world with your arms as an octopus does? Smell the pheromonic subtleties in air as a moth can?

Heather Swan, poetry editor: In thinking about the poets I wanted to invite to contribute to Sensoria, I thought of those whose embodied knowledge of the world, human and more-than-human, seems to scaffold their poetry. Poetic language is always trying to lift the reader out of the lull of everyday conversation to new poignant awareness, to wake the reader up. I feel that returning to the senses in this moment is so crucial, and the poems are an invitation to do so.

Source: Humans & Nature Press/used with permission.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

GVH: At the Center for Humans & Nature, which is where I work, our mission is to explore and promote human responsibilities in relation to nature—the whole community of life. All the books we publish at Humans & Nature Press, in creative ways, revolve around what it means to become a good creature, to become kin on a shared planet, and to expand our empathic imaginations.

HS: I am a poet, a nonfiction writer, a teacher, a human who is deeply aware of the miracle of the natural world as well as the devastation that is unfolding around us. Much of what is occurring in the world, in my opinion, seems to come from disconnection with our bodies, our hearts, with each other, and with the wild beings around us. A way to reconnect is through the senses.

This book aims to enliven and astonish, to make us prick up our ears, stare into rivers, listen to the hum of bumblebees working the flowers, taste the salt of the sea on our tongues, imagine what it might be to walk the Earth as a four-legged being, and in the process awaken to the beauty of this planet and to advocate for what is left.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

HS: This book is for everyone who wants to live a richer, more just, embodied life.

GVH: At the Center for Humans & Nature, we like to say we try to reach “the naturally curious,” people who love learning about the connections between ourselves and the living world. We are also a big round table for disciplinary boundary crossers, creative storytellers, and innovative ecological thinkers.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

GVH: The contributors to Sensoria approach their subject matter in three ways: 1) how humans can develop and sharpen our sensory capacities; 2) the ways other-than-human species experience the world differently than we do; and 3) the collective meaning-making that occurs between species and within living landscapes.

So there are stories about elephant funerary rituals, honeybees’ sense of beauty, the osmospheres of canine companions, and how it might change your perceptual set to get kicked in the head by a mule (courtesy of Gary Paul Nabhan), among so many others. As our perceptions are honed, things that were once “invisible” become visible; things unheard suddenly register. A more heightened sensitivity can refresh what we experience, in the sense that what once was dismissed or ignored as ordinary becomes extraordinary. Sensoria is also a reminder that the world is not for humans alone, nor are we alone within it.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

GVH: Sensoria is a collective project, with 50 essayists and poets from various geographies, fields of expertise and practice, and walks of life. There have been some fantastic books about other animals’ umwelts and special relationships between individual humans and particular species. However, we are proud to have created a book that looks to the wisdom of the collective. I would also say Sensoria is unusual in honoring poets as much as essayists and seeing how those different types of writing amplify and nuance one another.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about what you call sensoria, it will broaden their moral imaginations and improve their relationships with the nonhuman world?

HS: The human way of being on this planet is only one of a multitude. By imagining other ways of knowing this world, as an octopus or honeybee or canine or a tree, we are expanding our own experience, perhaps learning humility and respect for all that developed before us, the beings who can be our teachers and who deserve to thrive as much as humans do.

GVH: As we look to other creatures, our fellow travelers on this wild planet, we extend our capacity for care. We apprehend more fully that this world is made up of diverse subjects, not lifeless, unfeeling objects. Sensoria is a call to listen with our whole selves—our bodies as sensitive instruments—within a larger planetary song.

item.title: Mental Health of 9/11 Response and Recovery Workers
item.description:
Trauma

Mental Health of 9/11 Response and Recovery Workers

We must never forget the previous and continuing consequences of 9/11 responders.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • On 11 September 2001, response and recovery workers gave everything they had to offer.
  • As a consequence, their mental (and physical) health suffered and continues to suffer.
  • They deserve all the healthcare they need, while their lessons should be applied today.

Twenty-five years ago today, terrorists hijacked four aircraft in the northeastern USA. They crashed two into the World Trade Center towers in New York City, setting both towers alight until they collapsed. They flew one into the Pentagon in Washington, D.C. The fourth aircraft was on its way to crash into a building, almost certainly in Washington, D.C., when passengers fought back and the plane hit the ground in rural Pennsylvania.

Everyone aboard the four planes died. Thanks to the passengers on the fourth plane, no one died on the ground in that crash. 125 people inside the Pentagon were killed. Over 2,000 people in and around the World Trade Center died on 9/11, while more than a dozen perished soon after from injuries sustained.

Steel from New York City’s World Trade Center forming the 9/11 memorial in Christchurch, New Zealand.
Source: Ilan Kelman

Hundreds of emergency responders died when the World Trade Center towers fell. They had not hesitated to enter the burning buildings, climbing dozens of floors to try to help people escape. Many were on their day off, but turned up to assist when they saw or heard what had happened. Some security personnel and responders had exited one of the buildings and then re-entered to aid more people.

In the following years, thousands of response and recovery workers had to fight for medical coverage to deal with injuries sustained on the day or with cancers and other illnesses acquired when they breathed in toxic materials released in the building collapses. For survivors, another toll which continues has been the mental health consequences.

Mental health impacts

At least 51 rescue or recovery workers at the World Trade Center died by suicide from 2003 to 2014. Many unknowns remain. This total is likely higher due to inadequate reporting. It is hard to determine how many others have thought about or attempted suicide.

It is also difficult to know how many might have considered self-harm or ended up self-harming irrespective of 9/11. Mental health support, especially talking openly about feelings and preventive interventions, is clouded by working cultures unwilling to admit that these issues exist. Many positive advances around the world for this topic in recent years do not override the experiences of those still dealing with 9/11.

Numerous other mental health impacts from being response or recovery workers across the 9/11 sites are documented. Sadly, it is the usual post-disaster diagnoses, including self-harm, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, substance use, and anxiety. These consequences have long been known, yet were not always considered when supporting the workers.

A challenge is the huge variety of people and their reactions, across different emergency services and within specific units. Some people thrive due to adversity, which reduces or averts their ongoing adverse mental health impacts. The importance of health systems is highlighted. Proper health care means identifying people with mental health concerns in order to redress those concerns before significant problems manifest. Then, they would not require a horrific catastrophe such as 9/11 to help them avoid the worst mental health impacts.

Helping those who help us

A quarter of a century later, it is not too late to help those who help us. Numerous survivors remain among the response and recovery workers, as well as their families. They deserve the best available mental health and physical health support.

Their experiences and those from the workers who died due to mental health conditions should be used to improve how we support response and recovery workers. It is not just about disasters. Emergency responders have high rates of mental health difficulties, many of which could and should be dealt with through prevention and monitoring. They should also receive immediate support and treatment when signs and symptoms emerge.

When we phone an emergency number, we expect trained and competent personnel to be available for us. We must be available for them, to help them through the terrible mental health (and physical health) implications of their jobs which save our lives.

item.title: 3 Reasons Struggling Adult Children Feel So Invisible
item.description:
Attention

3 Reasons Struggling Adult Children Feel So Invisible

They may get the most attention in the family, and still feel unseen.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • A struggling adult child's problems gradually becomes their identity within the family
  • Even well-intended parental help can feel like a constant performance review
  • Shame can make expressed concern feel like oppressive judgment

Stefanie (altered names throughout to protect privacy) said the following to me in a recent parent coaching session: "Dr. Jeff, I don't freaken (substitute word here too, just use your imagination) get it! Jimmy (Stefanie's 29-year-old son) gets all my attention, more than anyone else in the family, and I am so freaken drained. I worry about him, offer guidance, give him money, and spend countless hours thinking about what I did to cause his problems."

Stefanie's words mirror so many parents who share those painful stories with me about their adult children. They, like Stefanie, also share this sense of a crazy contradiction. Why is it that these parents care so much and do so much, and yet their adult children say things like: "You don't understand me." "All you do is invalidate me. Everyone thinks I'm a loser." So how can these adult children, who get so much attention, feel so invisible?

Below are three reasons why adult children feel unseen when all their parents see is themselves doing everything.

1. Their Struggle Has Become Their Identity

The same adult child struggling many years ago was born alongside their parents' hopes and dreams for them. Yet when an adult child struggles emotionally, educationally, financially, employment-wise, or fails to develop relationships, the family conversations can easily slide into what is wrong. And then there are the questions that adult children feel like they are pummeled with, such as "Did you apply for that job? or "How are your finances holding up?" or "Any updates on trying to go back to college?" or (this is the killer), "So, what's your plan?"

What I am saying is that I see parents who know everything about the struggles but, surprisingly, very little about what their adult child is thinking, wondering, laughing about, or hoping for. No, I am not blaming all this on the parents. But couldn't a more useful question for parents to ask be something like: "When was the last time I had a conversation with my adult child that wasn't about improving their life?"

2. Help Starts To Feel Like a Performance Review

How can parents of struggling adult children not feel some anxiety? Of course they do. But the problem with anxiety, especially when it ramps up, is that it creates urgency, and that urgency makes us want to fix things. So, these well-meaning parents offer ideas (in the form of unsolicited advice) like: "Hey, why don't you apply to more places? Or, "Have you called them back?" Or, "You know, you should get out of the house more." Or, "Maybe you should tell that to your therapist."

The kicker here is that many of these suggestions are reasonable. But when an adult child feels like crap about where they truly are in life (at least the ones I speak with do), these repeated attempts to give guidance feel like on-the-spot performance evaluations. I'm not saying parents should never give advice, but before offering another solution, ask, "Do you want my ideas, or do you just want me to listen right now?"

3. Shame Can Make Concern Feel Like Judgment

When writing my book for parents of struggling adult children entitled, You Ruined My Life Now You Owe Me, I had the opportunity to reflect deeply. I asked myself, "Imagine what it is like being 31 and seeing friends get promoted, married, or buy their first homes while you are still living with your parents. Or, being 34 and starting over after another job falls apart.

Or maybe an adult child has a solid career but feels desperately lonely because they can't form a lasting relationship. Social media these days certainly amplifies these negative comparisons to others. This is why struggling adult children often react defensively to questions that parents genuinely mean as concern. Deep down, they are feeling, "Please don't remind me of how far behind I already feel."

In Closing: The Best Question To Help Your Adult Child Feel Seen

Okay, there may not be a best question, but my parent coaching clients frequently tell me this one really helps: "What's the hard part of what you're going through that you don't think I understand?" Then, do the hardest part: Listen, really listen. Don't defend yourself or explain what they should do next; just listen.
